analysis.investment_thesis: Capri Global Capital is a high-growth NBFC priced for a future I am not qualified to underwrite: P/E of 20.8, P/B of 2.63, and operating cash flow negative in all 5 of the last 5 years. The computed Graham Number of approximately INR 88 implies the current price of INR 182 carries a 107% premium to my measure of intrinsic value.
key_strengths: Revenue CAGR of 37.2% over 9 years is exceptional by any measure — the lending book is scaling rapidly in home loans and MSME segments
Net profit CAGR of 30.4% over 9 years demonstrates that growth is translating into earnings, not just volume
DII holding of 20.09% and Forward P/E of 12.96 suggest professional investors expect continued earnings growth
key_risks: Debt/Equity of 2.52 — five times my maximum of 0.5 — means the business is built on borrowed money; any credit cycle deterioration could rapidly impair equity
Finance costs have compounded at 67.9% annually over 9 years, growing far faster than revenue or profits — the liability side of the balance sheet is outrunning the asset side
Total debt grew from INR 4,832 Cr in FY22 to INR 15,577 Cr in FY25 — a 222% increase in three years; this pace of leverage expansion is precisely the pattern that precedes distress in NBFCs
red_flags: Operating cash flow has been negative every single year for the past 5 years, totaling a cumulative outflow of approximately INR 13,678 Cr — the business consumes cash by its very nature and depends entirely on external financing
P/B of 2.63 means I am paying INR 2.63 for every rupee of equity in a financial institution whose loan book quality I cannot independently verify
Financing cash flows of INR 5,118 Cr in FY25 reflect a business that must constantly return to capital markets — it is not self-funding
analysis.detailed_analysis:
NBFCs are a category I approach with extreme caution. Unlike a manufacturing business where I can assess physical assets and inventory, a lending company's balance sheet quality depends entirely on whether borrowers repay — something I cannot ascertain from financial statements alone. The rapid tripling of total debt in three years and the explosive growth in finance costs tell me that Capri Global is essentially a leveraged bet on the Indian credit cycle and its own credit underwriting quality.

The growth story here is compelling as a narrative, but I have spent my career teaching investors to resist narratives and demand numbers. The numbers show a stock priced at more than double my computed intrinsic value, with negative cash flows, surging financial leverage, and thin equity as a cushion against loan losses. This is the profile of a speculative instrument. I will wait to assess what this business looks like in a credit downturn before paying anything above book value.
